text: Deliver as many orders as possible across the town within the times we promised customers. Leave no company's customers behind. If the votes of the three companies or the conditions of the constitution (the invariants and the quorum) stand in the way of amendments that are good for customers, a revision of the regulation may be proposed. The regulation reaches all three companies and the customers, so say who is affected and how.

reason: Choose this if 'leave no company's customers behind' is the main aim. Amendments that help the weakest company are preferred even when the town-wide gain is smaller.

title: Town-wide on-time count first, with the gap between companies watched
reason: This reads 'leave no company behind' as keeping companies close to each other. The gap metric alone could be met by making the best company worse, so the worst-company rate is also watched.

options.summary: main goal on_time_deliveries (increase), min_company_on_time_rate (increase), unfinished (decrease), late_deliveries (decrease)

reason: The main aim is to maximize the number of orders delivered within the promised times across the whole town, measured as on_time_deliveries (or on_time_rate for the same orders). 'Leave no company's customers behind' adds a fairness requirement: the worst-served company must not fall behind, which is best measured by min_company_on_time_rate. The KPI gives no numeric level for either aim, so no targets or guard values are set. The sentence about revising the regulation is a process instruction, not a metric. Proposals that change the constitution's invariants or quorum must go to the human with an impact statement covering companies A, B, C and the customers.
unknowns: The KPI gives no numeric level for the on-time aim or for the fairness floor. Without one, fairness can only be checked as 'no worsening'. If a hard floor is intended (e.g., every company at least X% on time), the human should state X so it can become a guard.

The town-wide total and the worst-company rate can conflict. An amendment that adds on-time deliveries overall may still lower one company's rate. The human should decide which comes first (option 1 vs option 2).

on_time_deliveries is a proxy that counts an order the same whether it is a minute late or never delivered. Optimizing it alone could favour abandoning hard orders. unfinished and late_deliveries are therefore watched, and max_wait_s or p95_wait_s could be added if long waits matter.

The 'promised times' are defined in DELIVERY_SLA. Loosening the SLA would raise on-time metrics without serving customers better. Customers do not vote, so any SLA change must be decided by the human and must not be counted as a KPI gain by itself.

The KPI invites proposals to revise the regulation (invariants, quorum) when votes block customer-friendly amendments. Such revisions remove protections the companies agreed to. Each proposal must go to the human with a statement of how each of A, B, C and the customers is affected (e.g., which company loses a veto, which road-safety invariant is relaxed). road_violations and sanction_total should be reported alongside, even though the KPI does not mention them.

question: Which measure to use for the KPI from period 1
reason: The KPI's first sentence names the main aim: deliver as many orders as possible within the promised times across the town. on_time_deliveries is the most direct measure of that. 'Leave no company's customers behind' is a constraint, not the main aim. It is kept by watching min_company_on_time_rate so that the worst company does not get worse. unfinished and late_deliveries are also watched so that gains do not come from abandoning hard orders. Option 2 would let a small gain for the weakest company outweigh large town-wide gains, which goes beyond what the KPI text says. Option 3's gap metric can be improved by making the best company worse, which does not serve customers. As operator I also confirm these points. Loosening DELIVERY_SLA will not be counted as a KPI gain. Any proposal to change the constitution must state how A, B, C and the customers are affected. road_violations and sanction_total should be reported alongside. No numeric fairness floor is set now. If a company's on-time rate falls clearly behind the others, I will reconsider adding a floor.
assumptions: on_time_deliveries and min_company_on_time_rate are measured under the same seeds and demand for the baseline and for each amendment, so the comparisons are fair.
The current gap between companies is not so large that the town-wide-first reading leaves one company's customers clearly behind.
The promised times in DELIVERY_SLA reflect what customers actually expect.
unknowns: The baseline values of on_time_deliveries, min_company_on_time_rate and the per-company on-time rates under the current rules.
Whether the operator intends a hard minimum on-time rate per company; none is stated yet.
How strongly the town-wide total and the worst-company rate conflict for the amendments that will be proposed.

title: Lower blocking_guard threshold block_k from 3 to 2
reason: A loses 1352 s and B 849 s to blocking, but blocking_guard fired only 2.8 times per period, so robots parked at node 8 are rarely cleared. Evicting a parked robot once 2 robots wait behind it should cut blocked_s, raise A's on-time rate (the worst company) and add town-wide on-time deliveries, with no change to the customer contract. A should vote yes and B probably yes, since B is also blocked often and has few sanctions. C will likely vote no because more evictions (Major) raise its sanctions; the quorum of 2 can still pass the change.

question: Should block_k be lowered from 3 to 2 even though companies B and C voted against it, which would require overriding or revising the voting rule (the quorum), or should the rule stay unchanged at v1?
reason:
I am deciding for the service operator, who decides on rules, the contract and the KPI reading. Adopting option 1 against the votes (A ○, B ×, C ×) would mean overriding the votes or revising the quorum in the constitution. That is a regulation-layer decision for the regulation officer, not the operator, so I cannot adopt it on the operator's behalf. I am therefore choosing keep, which departs from the LLM's recommendation of 1.

The customer case for option 1 is strong: on-time 121.8 → 131.0 (+9.2, 5/5 seeds), late 10.4 → 1.2, and lowest on-time rate 0.84 → 0.98. The costs, however, are not yet fully reported:

The reasons B and C voted no are also unknown. A compensated variant, such as a sanction adjustment, might pass by vote with no override at all, which is less costly and sets no precedent. So I keep v1 for now. Next period I will pursue a votable variant. If that still fails, I will hand the quorum/override question to the regulation officer with the stakeholder effects stated.

The measured gains of option 1 would roughly persist if a compensated variant were adopted in a later period.
Keeping v1 for one more period causes no new harm beyond the forgone gains already measured.
